title: Tone sandhi in Hokkien
content:
繁體中文
简体中文

In Hokkien, a character’s tone can change depending on where it appears.

The basic rule is simple:

If a character is last, it keeps its original tone. If another character comes right after it, the tone changes.

Just remember these three terms:

Citation tone = the original tone, like how the word is read by itself.
Sandhi tone = the changed tone when another character follows.
Neutral tone = a light tone with no tone mark.

This guide uses Tangliengim to explain how these mechanisms work, and specifically follows the Taipei tone sandhi pattern.1


  1. Tone legend
  2. Sandhi pattern
    i. Character type & punctuation
    ii. Neutral tone
    iii. Verbs ending in noun characters
    iv. Sandhi in noun-characters
    v. Verb-noun-verb constructions

1. Tone legend

Hokkien is represented with five tones in the Tangliengim system. The five tone marks used here are:

¹ IPA 44 ˦ & 4 ˦; POJ Tone 1 and Tone 8 (merged in Tangliengim notation)
² IPA 53 ˥˧; POJ Tone 2
³ IPA 21 ˨˩ & 32 ˧˨; POJ Tone 3 and Tone 4 (merged in Tangliengim notation)
⁴ IPA 214 ˨˩˦; POJ Tone 5
⁵ IPA 22 ˨; POJ Tone 7

2. Sandhi pattern

When a tone changes, it follows the pattern below. The examples given in this article will also show how the pattern works in practice.

i. Character type & punctuation

Some characters behave like nouns. These are noun-characters (N). They often prefer to keep their original tone, even when another character follows.

Everything else is marked as X. These are usually verbs, adjectives, prepositions, and other non-noun-characters. When another character follows, they usually change tone.

Spaces and punctuation are not just decoration. They tell you where a phrase ends. The character right before a space, comma, period, or ’ keeps its original tone.

Examples:

ˎ 릐 lì N     킈 khi X .
‘You go.’

릐ˎ is citation with a space before it. 킈 is citation because it is final.

Citation tone Sandhi tone N Noun-character X Non-noun-character
ˎ 꽈 goà N   ˎ 킈 khì- X   쿤 khun X .
‘I go to sleep.’

꽈ˎ is citation with a space behind it. 킈 is sandhi (킈 → 킈ˎ) because 쿤 comes directly after it. 쿤 is citation because it is final.

ˏ 랑 láng N     쟣 jiah- X ˍ 븡 pn̄g N .
‘People eat rice.’

랑ˏ is citation with a space behind it. 쟣ꞈ undergoes (checked tone) sandhi (쟣ꞈ → 쟣) with 븡ˍ directly attached after it. 븡ˍ is citation because it is final.

ii. Neutral tone

Neutral tone, simply put, is a tone in which a character is deemphasised and pronounced quickly at a low pitch.

a. Particles

Particle words that come after ’ like ’에 (’e), ’롷킈 (’loh-khi) and ’짇에 (’jit-e) lose their tone marks and become neutral. Exception: ’ᄅᆤˎ (liàu) keeps its Falling Tone/Tone 2.

After a ’ phrase, put a space or punctuation before the next normal word. This shows that the neutral part has ended. You can also stack several neutral particles after the same ’.

Examples:

ˎ 릐 lì N ’   에 ’e X   ˏ 먀 miá N
‘your name’

에ˏ became neutral (에ˏ → 에) because it comes after ’. 먀ˏ is citation because it starts a new phrase after the space (and is the last character).

ꞈ 림 lîm X ’   롷 ’loh- X   킈 khi- X   에 e X   ˎ 쥐 jùi N
‘the water that was drunk (down)’

Everything after ’ is neutral until the spacing. 쥐ˎ is citation because the space before it starts a new normal word (and is the last character).

Citation tone Neutral tone N Noun-character X Non-noun-character

The character before ’ is treated like it is phrase-final. So it keeps its original tone.

Note for mixed-script writing: write particles after ’ in Hangul, not Hanri (漢字한`띠ˉ; Chinese characters). This makes the neutral-tone part easy to see.

b. Pronouns

Pronouns can also become neutral when they are the object of a sentence (accusative position), appearing after ’.

Example:

ˎ 꽈 goà N     애 ai X ’   릐 ’li N .
‘I love you.’

릐ˎ) is neutral because it comes after ’. It loses its tone mark.

Citation tone Neutral tone N Noun-character X Non-noun-character

iii. Verbs ending in noun-characters

Some verbs, such as 재ˍ얄ˎ (jāi-yà̰, “to know”) and 탁쳏 (thak-cheh, “to study“), end in a noun-character, so their final character does not undergo tone sandhi in a sentence. Tone behaviour is still determined character by character.

Example:

ˎ 꽈 goà N   ˍ 재 jāi- X ˎ 얄 yà̰ N   ˍ 이 ī N ’   에 ’e X   ˏ 먀 miá N .
‘I know his name.’

Since 재ˍ얄ˎ is formed by combining non-noun-character 재ꞈ and noun-character 얄ˎ, 재ꞈ underwent tone sandhi (재ꞈ → 재ˍ) while 얄ˎ does not.

Citation tone Sandhi tone Neutral tone N Noun-character X Non-noun-character

iv. Sandhi in noun-characters

Noun-characters usually resist tone change, but they are not immune. If an N character is glued tightly into a larger word, name, or fixed expression, it can change tone too.

Example:

ˎ 진 jìn- N ꞈ 덩 tông N     쟣 jiah- X ˎ 궤 kuè N .
‘Jìn-tông (name) eats kuè.’

In 진ˎ덩ꞈ, 진 changes tone (진 → 진ˎ) because it is glued to 덩ꞈ as one phrase.

Citation tone Sandhi tone N Noun-character X Non-noun-character

If a postposition is attached to a noun character, the noun character undergoes tone sandhi.

Example:

ꞈ 쥐 jûi- N ˍ 래 lāi N
‘in the water’

쥐ˎ is a noun-character, but undergoes tone sandhi (쥐ˎ → 쥐ꞈ) due to the attached postposition –래ˍ (meaning ‘in’).

Citation tone Sandhi tone N Noun-character X Non-noun-character

v. Verb-noun-verb constructions

Sometimes a noun-character gets trapped inside a verb phrase. When that happens, it can change tone too.

Example:

ˍ 턀 thiā̰- X   랑 lang- N ˎ 겅 kòng X
‘to hearsay’

턀ˍ랑겅ˎ literally means ‘hear people say,’ but together it acts like ‘hearsay.’ Because 랑ˏ is stuck inside the phrase, it changes tone (랑ˏ → 랑).

Citation tone Sandhi tone N Noun-character X Non-noun-character
